idiom_name: Thread::Queue instance per message type (cross-process: Sidekiq queue per job class)
implementation_notes: Thread::Queue is Ruby's core multi-producer/multi-consumer channel: since it is untyped, the datatype channel is realized as one queue object per message type plus one consumer loop per queue, with the type carried by the queue's identity (constant or attribute) rather than by the payload. The dominant cross-process form is the Sidekiq convention that each worker/job class has its own queue name which workers list explicitly - a channel per message type in all but name, and the reason a misconfigured queue name silently routes work nowhere. Where the boundary is typed at all, validate in the job's perform method (or push value objects only); Thread::Queue itself will accept anything.
code_sketch:
ORDERS   = Thread::Queue.new        # one queue per message type
INVOICES = Thread::Queue.new

Thread.new { loop { handle_order(ORDERS.pop) } }
ORDERS << Order.new(id: 42)         # no type tag in the payload

# cross-process equivalent:
# class BillingJob; sidekiq_options queue: 'invoices'; end
pitfalls: Thread::Queue is untyped: pushing a Hash onto ORDERS is accepted and blows up in the consumer, so wrap the queue in a small facade that validates if the contract matters.
An in-process queue dies with the process; durable per-type channels need Sidekiq queue names (or Redis Streams/Kafka topics), while Thread::Queue is only for hand-off inside one runtime.
pop blocks forever and there is no retry or dead-letter: a consumer thread that raises loses the element unless the broker behind the channel (Sidekiq's per-job retry) provides those semantics.
